groups.label: Utopian & Political Commentary
groups.summary: Commentary examines Plato's political works alongside historical and philosophical counterparts, comparing the Republic and Laws, exploring governance in the Statesman, and analyzing ideal societies across Cicero, Augustine, Dante, and Campanella.
groups.rationale: These entries form a continuous sequence of editorial introductory commentary examining Platonic dialogues and comparative political treatises across history.

groups.label: Traditional Views of Justice
groups.summary: Cephalus connects character and wealth in old age to peace of mind, prompting Socrates to refute the idea of justice as simply repaying debts before Polemarchus redefines it as aiding friends and harming enemies.
groups.rationale: These entries cover the opening philosophical conversation of Book I, transitioning from Cephalus's conventional reflections on life and debt to Polemarchus's traditional definition of justice.

groups.label: Debate with Thrasymachus
groups.summary: Socrates argues rulers may err against their own interest, while Thrasymachus claims injustice is stronger and more profitable than justice, concluding with the acknowledgment of justice as the soul's excellence and Socrates's dissatisfaction.
groups.rationale: These entries encompass the core clash with Thrasymachus in Book I regarding whether injustice is virtue and profit, concluding with an editorial sidenote on the outcome of the argument.

groups.label: Book II Challenges & State Analogy
groups.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus challenge Socrates to defend justice for its intrinsic worth rather than its external gains or reputations, leading Socrates to propose examining justice first in the larger context of the State.
groups.rationale: These entries form the unified opening movement of Book II, starting with the brothers' revived challenge against justice and culminating in Socrates's proposed macro-micro method of political inquiry.
